content: Giardia cysts have been detected in raw sewage at concentrations of up to 240 cysts per liter and in surface water resources. These cysts are highly resilient and can persist in freshwater environments for weeks to months. Their presence has been confirmed in both raw water sources and drinking water supplies, although it remains unclear whether the species detected are infectious to humans. Current standard analytical methods only provide indirect assessments of cyst viability and do not determine their infectivity to humans. Giardia cysts are also found in recreational waters and contaminated food. The most common route of Giardia transmission is person-to-person contact, particularly among children. Outbreaks have also been linked to contaminated drinking water, recreational water, and, to a lesser extent, food. Animals have been implicated as potential sources of human-infectious Giardia intestinalis, but further research is needed to clarify their role. Waterborne outbreaks of giardiasis have been associated with drinking water supplies for over 30 years. At one point, Giardia was the most frequently identified cause of waterborne outbreaks in the United States. Giardia cysts are more resistant to oxidative disinfectants like chlorine than enteric bacteria but are less resistant than Cryptosporidium oocysts. For example, achieving 90% inactivation of Giardia cysts with a free chlorine residual of 1 mg/L requires approximately 25–30 minutes. Effective control measures within a water safety plan include preventing contamination of source water by human and animal waste, followed by adequate treatment, disinfection, and protection of water during distribution. Due to the cysts' resistance to disinfectants, Escherichia coli (or thermotolerant coliforms) cannot reliably indicate the presence or absence of Giardia in drinking water supplies. Isospora belli is a coccidian, single-celled, obligate parasite related to Cryptosporidium and Cyclospora. It infects humans exclusively, undergoing both asexual and sexual reproduction in the mucosal epithelium of the upper small intestine. Sporulated oocysts are ingested, and unsporulated oocysts are excreted in feces. Illness caused by I. belli resembles that caused by Cryptosporidium and Giardia. Symptoms, which appear about one week after ingestion of viable oocysts, include low-grade fever, fatigue, malaise, mild diarrhea, and vague abdominal pain. The infection is usually self-limiting within 1–2 weeks but can persist for 6 weeks to 6 months in some cases. Symptomatic isosporiasis is more common in children and immunocompromised individuals, where it can lead to chronic or recurrent symptoms, malabsorption, and weight loss. Infections are most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions but have also been reported in industrialized countries. Unsporulated oocysts of I. belli are excreted in the feces of infected individuals and sporulate in the environment within 1–2 days, becoming infectious. Data on the prevalence of oocysts in sewage and water sources are limited due to the lack of sensitive and reliable detection methods. Poor sanitation and fecally contaminated food and water are the most likely sources of infection, although waterborne transmission has not been confirmed. Freshly shed oocysts require environmental sporulation before becoming infectious, making direct person-to-person transmission less likely. The characteristics of I. belli suggest that illness could be transmitted via contaminated drinking water, but this has not been confirmed. The organism is likely resistant to disinfectants but may be easier to remove by filtration due to its larger size compared to Cryptosporidium. Microsporidia are eukaryotic, obligate intracellular parasites belonging to the phylum Microspora. Although initially classified as protozoa, recent studies suggest they may be more closely related to fungi. Over 100 microsporidial genera and nearly 1,000 species have been identified, infecting a wide range of vertebrates and invertebrates. Several genera, including Enterocytozoon, Encephalitozoon, Nosema, and Pleistophora, have been implicated in human infections. Microsporidia are among the smallest eukaryotes, measuring 1–5 µm, and possess a coiled polar filament for injecting the sporoplasm into host cells. Within infected cells, they undergo complex multiplication processes, producing new spores that are excreted in feces, urine, respiratory secretions, or other body fluids, depending on the species and site of infection. Microsporidia are emerging human pathogens, primarily identified in individuals with AIDS, although they can also cause disease in immunocompetent hosts. Human infections have been reported worldwide. In AIDS patients, the most common clinical manifestation is severe enteritis with chronic diarrhea, dehydration, and weight loss, which can persist for up to 48 months. Infections in the general population are less severe. Enterocytozoon infections are generally limited to intestinal enterocytes and biliary epithelium, while Encephalitozoon species infect a variety of cell types, including epithelial and endothelial cells, fibroblasts, kidney tubule cells, and macrophages. Unusual complications include keratoconjunctivitis, myositis, and hepatitis. The sources of microsporidia infecting humans are uncertain. Spores are likely excreted in feces, urine, and respiratory secretions. Limited data exist on the prevalence of microsporidia spores in water environments, but they have been detected in sewage and water sources. Their numbers in raw sewage may be similar to those of Cryptosporidium and Giardia, and they may survive in certain water environments for months. Swine and other animals may serve as hosts for human-infectious species. Transmission routes are poorly understood but likely include person-to-person contact and ingestion of spores in contaminated water or food. A waterborne outbreak of microsporidiosis involving approximately 200 cases occurred in Lyon, France, in 1995, although the source of contamination was not identified. Airborne transmission via inhalation of spores or aerosols is also possible. The role of animals in human transmission remains unclear. Naegleria fowleri is a free-living amoeboflagellate widely distributed in the environment. It exists in three stages: trophozoite, flagellate, and cyst. The trophozoite (10–20 µm) moves via eruptive pseudopods, feeds on bacteria, and reproduces by binary fission. It can transform into a flagellate stage with two anterior flagella, which does not divide but reverts to the trophozoite stage. Under adverse conditions, the trophozoite forms a circular cyst (7–15 µm) resistant to unfavorable conditions. N. fowleri causes primary amoebic meningoencephalitis (PAM) in healthy individuals. The amoeba enters the brain by penetrating the olfactory mucosa and cribriform plate. The disease is acute, with patients often dying within 5–10 days before the infectious agent can be diagnosed. Treatment is challenging, and new cases are reported annually despite the rarity of the infection. N. fowleri is thermophilic, thriving at temperatures up to 45°C. It occurs naturally in warm freshwater environments, with prevalence indirectly influenced by human activities that modify temperature or promote bacterial growth. The pathogen has been reported in many countries, often associated with thermally polluted water environments such as geothermal water or heated swimming pools. It has also been detected in drinking water supplies, particularly where water temperatures exceed 25–30°C. Water is the only known source of infection. Since the first cases of amoebic meningitis were diagnosed in 1965 in Australia and Florida, approximately 100 cases of PAM have been reported worldwide.
